# Maria's Story

Maria has worked at the same Italian restaurant in the downtown core for nearly twelve years. She knows the regulars by name, remembers their usual orders, and takes pride in the way she moves through the dining room—efficient, warm, present. For most of her career, she has loved this work. The rhythm of service, the small moments of connection with guests, the camaraderie with her kitchen staff: these things have sustained her through her divorce five years ago and the loneliness that followed.

Three years ago, a man began coming in every Friday evening. He would sit at one of her tables, order the same dish, and watch her work. At first, Maria thought nothing of it. Regular customers are common. But his attention felt different. He would wait for her after her shifts ended, appearing in the parking lot or standing across the street. He knew details about her life she had never shared—where she lived, when she went to the gym, that she had a sister in Sacramento. When she asked him to stop, he said he was simply admiring her, that he meant no harm. The restaurant manager told her she was overreacting.

The behavior escalated. He began leaving notes tucked into her apron pocket, showing up at her apartment building, calling her phone from different numbers. One evening, she found him sitting in his car outside her home at two in the morning. When she called the police, they took a report but told her there was little they could do without a direct threat. For months, Maria lived in a state of constant vigilance. She changed her routes to work. She installed new locks. She stopped going to the gym. She stopped leaving her apartment on days she wasn't working.

Eventually, through persistence and documentation, a restraining order was granted. He was arrested. He served three months. That was two years ago.

But Maria has not returned to herself.

She still works at the restaurant, but something fundamental has shifted. She startles at unexpected voices or touches, even when a regular guest places a gentle hand on her shoulder to get her attention. Last week, a new customer sat at one of her tables and made consistent eye contact while ordering. Maria's hands trembled as she wrote down his order. She excused herself to the bathroom and stood there for fifteen minutes, her heart racing, telling herself he was just a normal person ordering dinner.

She has difficulty sleeping. When she does drift off, she dreams of being followed, of doors that won't lock, of voices calling her name from outside her window. She wakes at three or four in the morning, her sheets soaked with sweat, and cannot fall back asleep. During the day, she feels exhausted and foggy, moving through her shift on autopilot.

Maria has become hyperaware of exits. She notes them in every room. She watches the faces of men who enter the restaurant, assessing threat levels, planning escape routes. She finds herself irritable with guests who linger too long at their tables, who ask for her attention repeatedly, who seem to look at her too intently. Twice in the past month, she has had to step outside because she felt like she couldn't breathe, her chest tightening as though the walls were closing in.

Her sister has suggested she find different work, but Maria resists. She has built a life here, and she is afraid that leaving would mean the stalker has taken something else from her. Yet each shift feels like a negotiation between her need for normalcy and the constant undercurrent of fear that something terrible might happen again.
